analysis.one_liner: Restores investors' right to sue for securities fraud by repealing 1990s lawsuit limits.
analysis.headline: Introduced months after the Enron collapse, the bill was sent to two House committees, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rolled back the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995 and a related 1998 law that make it much harder for investors to sue companies over securities fraud. It would have restored class-action rights, ended special protections for companies' public predictions, reopened lawsuits against people who help commit fraud (like auditors and bankers), protected whistleblowers who tip off lawsuits, and let investors sue up to three years after discovering a fraud. It never received a hearing or a vote in either committee it was sent to.
analysis.who_benefits: Shareholders and employees whose savings sit in company stock or retirement funds would regain practical ways to recover losses from securities fraud. Whistleblowers who provide the facts behind a fraud lawsuit would no longer have their identity exposed in court filings. Plaintiffs' lawyers who take securities-fraud cases would get a much larger docket of viable claims.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Investors and employees with company stock

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the provisions of the 1995 reform law that limit private securities class actions, cap damages, shield companies' forward-looking predictions, and shield outside directors with only proportionate liability, making it easier for defrauded investors to sue and recover full losses [S2] [S3].

Restores liability for people who knowingly or recklessly help commit securities fraud — such as auditors, accountants, and advisers — across the securities, investment company, and investment adviser laws [S2] [S3].
Changes the fraud-pleading rules so a complaint based on information and belief does not have to name its sources, protecting whistleblowers who supply tips about corporate misconduct [S2] [S3].
Extends the time limit for suing on securities fraud to three years after the violation was discovered, covering frauds that surface slowly [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Publicly traded companies, their executives and directors, accounting and audit firms, banks, and investment advisers would face greater exposure to investor lawsuits and larger potential damages. Shareholders as a group would also indirectly bear some higher litigation and settlement costs that companies pass through.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the 'safe harbor' for corporate predictions and the limits on strike suits would expose companies to lawsuits over honest business forecasts, the problem the 1995 law was written to curb [S2] [S3].

The bill repeals court-ordered security for costs and the sanctions and pleading safeguards against abusive litigation, which could raise the volume of weak suits and the litigation costs that companies — and ultimately all their shareholders — pay [S2] [S3].

Restoring full joint liability would mean deep-pocketed defendants like auditors and banks could be sued for entire fraud judgments even for small roles, an exposure the 1995 law's proportionate-liability rules were designed to prevent [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For investors who lost retirement savings to fraud like Enron's, the bill offered a genuine remedy: the 1995 law's strict pleading rules, damages caps, and safe harbor made many fraud cases practically unwinnable, and this bill removed all of them. The honest cost is that a full repeal rather than a recalibration also reopens the door to weak strike suits that settle rather than fight, and those settlement costs are paid largely out of the pockets of the very shareholders the bill is trying to protect. A more targeted bill might have balanced those goals; a full repeal does not.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced months after the Enron collapse made securities fraud a national issue, the bill was referred to the Financial Services and Judiciary committees and then to two subcommittees, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended; Congress instead passed narrower corporate-reform legislation later that year.

narrative.text: Rep. Bart Stupak introduced the bill on February 28, 2002, with Rep. John LaFalce, and it was referred to the Financial Services Committee and the Judiciary Committee the same day [S1] [S3] [S5].
On March 18, 2002, portions were referred to the Capital Markets subcommittee of Financial Services and the Courts subcommittee of Judiciary; no further action was ever recorded [S5] [S1].
The bill attracted only one cosponsor in the 435-member House and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote in either chamber [S4] [S5].
The 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, and all bills not passed by then die automatically [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations, their executives, auditors, and the financial firms the bill would have exposed to lawsuits kept the lawsuit shields of the 1995-98 laws intact. Defrauded investors and employees with company stock got no new remedy from this bill; the corporate-reform law Congress did pass that year left those lawsuit limits in place.

for.name: Rep. Bart Stupak
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the securities-lawsuit limits and referred it to two committees

for.name: Rep. John LaFalce
for.role: U.S. Representative, New York; original cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor at introduction

against.name: House Financial Services and Judiciary Committees
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on any part of it

against.name: Accounting firms and financial industry groups
against.role: Industries protected by the 1995 and 1998 lawsuit limits
against.what_they_did: Publicly defended the existing limits on investor lawsuits, which shielded them from aiding-and-abetting and class-action liability, during the post-Enron reform debate

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken in either chamber; the bill's only two sponsors were Democrats, and it died in committees run by the Republican majority without any recorded floor division.

industries.industry: Publicly traded corporations and their executives
industries.note: The bill repeals the damages caps, safe harbor, and class-action limits that shield companies and their officers from investor fraud suits. Their interest in keeping those shields runs directly against defrauded investors' ability to recover.

The bill restores liability for knowingly or recklessly assisting a securities violation, squarely aimed at auditors and accountants who signed off on frauds like Enron's. Current law shields them from most such private suits.

industries.industry: Securities industry: brokerages, banks, and investment advisers
industries.note: Aiding-and-abetting liability would reach banks, advisers, and others who knowingly or recklessly assist fraud, exposing firms that profited from facilitating misconduct to private lawsuits.
Repealing the pleading, stay, and damages limits would greatly expand the pool of viable securities-fraud cases, and lawyers' fortunes in this area rise and fall with investors' access to the courts.
